title: Subset Sum below the meet-in-the-middle exponent
formal: Do there exist constants \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\), \(c\ge1\) and a uniform classical bounded-error randomized algorithm deciding whether a subset of \(n\) positive integers sums to a nonnegative integer target in \(O(2^{(1/2-\varepsilon)n}L^{c})\) worst-case time, where \(L\) is the total binary input length?
why: A fixed worst-case exponent improvement would break one of the best-known barriers for exact algorithms on a fundamental weakly NP-complete problem.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. The SODA 2026 paper retains the worst-case classical exponential question; the August 2026 preprint improves a quantum bound instead. No classical fixed-saving worst-case algorithm or unconditional impossibility proof for this model was located. The new quantum proof was not independently verified.

category_assignment.reason: The target is worst-case exponential time parameterized by the number of input items.

importance.reason: A fixed worst-case exponent improvement would break one of the best-known barriers for exact algorithms on a fundamental weakly NP-complete problem.

definitions: The input is \(n\ge1\), a target \(t\ge0\), and an explicitly listed multiset \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\) of positive integers, all in binary with delimiters; \(L\) is the bit length of that full encoding. Accept if and only if there is \(I\subseteq[n]\) with \(\sum_{i\in I}x_{i}=t\). Each index is used at most once, repetitions of values are permitted, and the empty subset is allowed. Use a uniform random-access machine with \(w=d(n+\lceil\log_{2}(L+2)\rceil)\)-bit words for fixed \(d\ge1\), large enough to address exponential memory. Unit-cost instructions are word read/write, copy, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, comparisons, Boolean operations and shifts; shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword integers are handled through charged component operations. Input packing, preprocessing and memory initialization are charged. Random words are independent and uniform and cost one instruction each. A fixed finite program receives no advice or tables. It answers correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input and the time bound holds on every random execution. Constants are independent of all input values and \(n,L\). Quantum operations and random-instance promises are absent.

context_blocks.text: Subset Sum asks whether some selection of the supplied indices adds to the target exactly. For values \((3,3,5)\), target \(6\) is attainable by taking both occurrences of \(3\); an occurrence cannot be used twice. Target zero is always attainable by the empty subset. The input multiplicities and the exact integer comparison are part of the problem.

The classical meet-in-the-middle benchmark is \(2^{n/2}\) times polynomial factors. The question asks for a smaller fixed exponential rate on every input, not an improvement in one polynomial factor. A bound such as \(2^{n/2}/n^{100}\) would still leave the requested exponent saving unresolved.

Pseudopolynomial algorithms depend on the numerical target rather than just the number of bits needed to write it. They can be excellent when the target is small, but binary input values can be exponentially large relative to their descriptions. Chan’s 2026 work improves this separate regime while explicitly retaining the worst-case exponential question.

An August 2026 preprint claims a quantum \(O^{\ast}(2^{2n/7})\) algorithm and still identifies the classical half-exponent benchmark. The star notation hides polynomial factors. The use of quantum computation is decisive: this does not supply the classical algorithm quantified over here. The new preprint proof was not independently checked.

Random instances, uniqueness promises and restrictions on the magnitude or density of the numbers can also alter exponential complexity. This target has none of those input promises and permits bounded-error classical randomness on every instance. Exponential memory is allowed and addressable in the specified RAM; a polynomial-space restriction would ask a different question.

answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one uniform classical randomized algorithm, constants \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), \(c\ge1\), and a constant multiplier meet the stated \(2^{(1/2-\varepsilon)n}L^c\) time bound on every random execution and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every input, or prove in Lean that no such choices exist. The theorem must allow unrestricted binary magnitudes, repeated positive values, all targets, and the full permitted RAM model.

sentences: Subset Sum asks whether some subcollection of given positive integers adds to a target.
The classical worst-case benchmark comes from the meet-in-the-middle exponent.
The question asks for a fixed positive saving in that exponent with polynomial dependence on binary input length.
Bounded-error classical randomization is allowed, with no random-instance promise.
Quantum, pseudopolynomial and polynomial-factor improvements do not establish this fixed exponent saving.
